transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Redwood - Lauren Kim (AE), Mateo Alvarez (SE); CartaHealth - Priya Singh (Head of ML), Ethan Brooks (Infra Lead), Maya Chen (Product), Samir Patel (SRE, joined late)

Summary (auto-generated): Reviewed caching hit rates and tuning options; plan benchmark and canonicalization work; share dashboards and schedule VPC/KMS follow-up.

Topics:
- Current cache hit rates (prefix vs KV)
- Prompt reuse / canonicalization strategies
- TTLs, eviction, and cache sizing per model
- Impact on latency and cost
- Next-step benchmarks and security/VPC concerns

Transcript:
[00:00] Lauren Kim: Okay, hi everyone, thanks for joining, um this is our weekly caching sync for the POC. I think we have the usual crew, Priya, Ethan, Maya — you all good?
[00:08] Priya Singh: Yep, good, thanks Lauren.
[00:10] Ethan Brooks: All good, joining from SF.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Hi, sorry team, just grabbing notes.
[00:15] Mateo Alvarez: Hey all, Mateo from Redwood infra, I'll run through the hit rates and the experiments we did this week.
[00:20] Lauren Kim: Great, Mateo over to you.

[00:30] Mateo Alvarez: Cool, real quick, so last week's config — we had prefix caching enabled with a 24-hour TTL and KV cache on a per-session basis. We ran live traffic sampling for three days and here's rough numbers, uh these are for the main chat workload you shared: prefix cache hit rate approximately 28 percent, KV cache around 12 percent. Combined effective token reuse was about 32 percent.
[00:54] Priya Singh: Wait, 28% prefix and 12% KV? That seems lower than we expected — we thought reuse would be higher given our templated prompts.
[01:02] Mateo Alvarez: Yeah, we saw that too. A couple of things — prompt variants and small micro-phrasing changes are busting the prefix keys. Also whitespace and punctuation differences, like, you know, someone adding a period or extra space. Tokenization boundary differences across models also change keys.
[01:18] Ethan Brooks: That matches what we see; front-end adds user metadata in the prompts sometimes. We didn't want to canonicalize everything early because product expects those fields for analytics.
[01:27] Maya Chen: Right, product needs some of that context inline for reranking, we can't strip everything.

[01:34] Mateo Alvarez: Totally — so a couple of strategies we tested: one, a conservative canonicalizer that normalizes whitespace, lowercases non-sensitive sections, and strips session-id like tokens; two, fuzzy keying where we hash only certain stable segments of the prompt; three, TTL tuning — longer TTLs increased hit rate slightly but caused stale prefix problems for dynamic instruction updates.
[01:55] Priya Singh: What was the impact of the canonicalizer on hit rate?
[01:58] Mateo Alvarez: With the conservative canonicalizer enabled on a sampled set we saw prefix hit rate jump from 28% to about 42% for that sample. KV went up a bit too — to about 18%. Latency median increased by maybe 5 to 10 ms due to extra CPU work for normalization, but for batch workloads it was negligible.
[02:18] Priya Singh: 42% is promising. Did you notice any quality regressions? Like, answers getting wrong because of canonicalization?
[02:24] Mateo Alvarez: We did human spot checks. Most of the time it's fine because canonicalizer only touches non-semantic parts. There were edge cases where entity capitalization mattered for fine-grained instructions — we flagged those.
[02:36] Lauren Kim: And TTL tuning — you said there were stale prefix problems?
[02:39] Mateo Alvarez: Yeah, longer TTLs helped reuse, but when your instruction templates change — for example, product updated the instruction layer on Friday — then when a cached prefix is stale the model sometimes follows old instructions. We saw a small uptick in wrong-behavior rates for the few routes that had instruction changes during the sample window.
[02:57] Maya Chen: That is a real concern for us — we do frequent instruction tweaks during experimentation.
[03:02] Priya Singh: Could we version keys? Like include an instruction-version token in the key so TTLs can be long but you invalidate by bumping the version?
[03:09] Mateo Alvarez: Absolutely, that was one of the proposals. Add a small instruction-version digest to the cache key. Then you get stable reuse and deterministic invalidation when you roll instructions.

[03:20] Ethan Brooks: On the infra side, what's the memory pressure like if we increase KV cache TTLs? We're concerned about cost on dedicated pools.
[03:27] Mateo Alvarez: Good question. For your POC traffic profile, doubling TTLs increases memory footprint by roughly 30% in our test. That's because KV entries are larger per session. We can size pools and also use eviction LRU tuned by request frequency. There's also tiered caching — keep hot prefixes in faster cache and others in a larger, slightly slower store.
[03:47] Priya Singh: Sounds reasonable. Can Redwood do per-model cache sizing automatically? We run a mix of 7B and 13B-ish models.
[03:55] Mateo Alvarez: Yes, the runtime supports per-model cache quotas and kernel optimizations. We can run heuristics — e.g., smaller models get smaller KV allocations. That was part of the Optimize feature set we suggested.

[04:05] Lauren Kim: Quick question about tokenization mismatches — you mentioned that earlier as a source of misses. Can you expand?
[04:11] Mateo Alvarez: Sure. When prompts are slightly different, the tokenizer splits can produce different token sequences, so prefix matching after tokenization fails. Our canonicalizer normalizes and then tokenizes to produce cache keys, but if you switch models with different tokenizers, keys won't line up. For cross-model reuse we need a shared keying strategy or limit reuse to compatible model family.
[04:33] Priya Singh: We're potentially going to test an alternative model family mid-POC, so that cross-model behavior matters.
[04:39] Mateo Alvarez: Right — we recommend either model-family-specific caches or a fallback route where if a cross-model miss happens we reroute to a lower-cost model or recompile. But cross-model caching is low-hanging fruit only within families where tokenizers and instruction semantics match.

[04:53] Maya Chen: On prompt reuse strategy — is Redwood recommending function-calling or structured inputs to reduce variance?
[04:59] Mateo Alvarez: Yes, structured inputs help a lot. If you can move dynamic fields into JSON fields and use the same instruction scaffolding, the textual prefix is very stable — hit rates go up substantially. Also leveraging function calls reduces surface area. We ran a small experiment with structured payloads and saw prefix hits ~55% on that route.
[05:18] Priya Singh: 55% — that's a big jump. But it would require changes to our product. Product team might be okay for high-traffic routes.

[05:28] Lauren Kim: OK, so to recap potential tactics: canonicalizer (conservative), instruction-versioning in keys, structured inputs where possible, per-model cache sizing, TTL tuning with invalidation on instruction revs. Anything missing?
[05:41] Mateo Alvarez: Also consider fuzzy keying and probabilistic matching for near-miss reuse — like allow keys with minor edit distance. That can increase reuse but risks semantic mismatch; needs careful thresholds.
[05:52] Ethan Brooks: How do we quantify the risk of semantic mismatch? We need a measurable guardrail.
[05:56] Mateo Alvarez: We can implement a QA sampling pipeline — every N cached hits, run a regression check against golden prompts and if mismatch rate exceeds threshold we auto-disable fuzzy matching for that route. We can tie this into your evals and log alerts in the console.

[06:14] Priya Singh: That seems sensible. On the benchmark side — what would the 10k request benchmark look like?
[06:20] Mateo Alvarez: We'll run synthetic traffic that mirrors your prompt families. Step one: Redwood to canonicalize sample prompts and run with current caching config; step two: enable canonicalizer and run again; step three: structured payload test. We'll capture latency p50/p95, token cost, and cache hit rates.
[06:35] Lauren Kim: We'll need help mapping your production prompt families, Priya can you provide that?
[06:40] Priya Singh: Yes, I'll export two weeks of anonymized prompt families — removing PII — and send them.

[06:45] Samir Patel: Sorry joining late — quick infra Q: for the VPC private deploy we were asking about KMS integration, does caching persist across restarts? How are keys secured?
[06:54] Mateo Alvarez: Caching persists if you attach persistent store (we support Redis or local SSD-backed stores in Private). Keys are application-layer cache keys, not encryption keys. For encryption at rest we integrate with customer KMS; the cache store can be encrypted. We also keep audit logs for cache write/read events.
[07:12] Ethan Brooks: Okay, on egress — we will need to pattern-match about what data leaves the VPC for hosted telemetry. We'll get back with constraints.

[07:20] Maya Chen: Any update on cost impact from caching — like token spend reduction?
[07:25] Mateo Alvarez: Based on the sample, effective token reduction was about 32% combined; with canonicalizer and structured inputs we project up to ~50% for targeted routes. That translates to proportional token cost savings; we'll quantify exactly in the benchmark.

[07:38] Priya Singh: That's helpful. One more question — does Redwood have an internal canonicalizer or would we build ours?
[07:45] Mateo Alvarez: We have a canonicalizer we use as a library. It's configurable; you can toggle rules per route. For POCs we propose Redwood run it as an intermediary layer in the proxy so you don't have to change client code initially. If you want to own it later we can hand over the config and helpers.

[07:59] Priya Singh: Could you share the canonicalizer rules and a sample mapping?
[08:03] Lauren Kim: Yes — action item, we'll share the ruleset and example mapping.

[08:10] Mateo Alvarez: Also worth noting — KV cache is very session-dependent. If your product sessions are short-lived, KV reuse will be low. For you, session median is about 18 minutes right?
[08:20] Priya Singh: Yeah, around there, many sessions are short.

[08:23] Mateo Alvarez: So focus on prefix caching and structured inputs for the higher wins.

[08:30] Ethan Brooks: For the benchmark, can you also surface which tokens are being reused? Like per-request token-level heatmaps? That would help us validate.
[08:38] Mateo Alvarez: Yup, we can provide per-request token reuse traces and a heatmap CSV. We'll also include the raw logs for a sample window.

[08:47] Maya Chen: Timeline question — how long to run the 10k benchmark and produce a report?
[08:51] Mateo Alvarez: The run itself will take a couple hours; analysis and report, 3 business days once we have canonicalized prompts and sample logs. So realistically by 2026-05-26 if we start early next week.

[09:03] Lauren Kim: Good. Any blockers from the customer side?
[09:06] Priya Singh: We need to extract logs and scrub PII; that might take a couple days. Also we need to align on which routes to prioritize.
[09:14] Maya Chen: Product can pick 2 high-traffic routes for structured input pilot.

[09:19] Lauren Kim: Perfect. Final recap: Redwood to share dashboard, canonicalizer rules, run 10k benchmark and provide token reuse traces; customer to provide anonymized prompts and pick pilot routes; schedule VPC/KMS follow-up to discuss security. Action items and due dates captured.
[09:36] Priya Singh: Thanks everyone.
[09:38] Ethan Brooks: Thanks.
[09:40] Mateo Alvarez: Thanks all, we'll follow up.

(Transcript ends)
